### Paycheck Calculator 2026

URL: https://greaterworldmedia.tech/paycheck-calculator/
Price: Free. Sign-up: not required. Processing: in your browser; files are not uploaded.

Convert hourly wage to annual salary and back, and estimate 2026 take-home pay per paycheck for any US state. Free, private, no sign-up.

Features:
- Hourly to salary and salary to hourly
- Overtime at 1.5x
- Weekly, biweekly, semimonthly or monthly paychecks
- 2026 federal and state income tax, Social Security and Medicare
- Pre-tax 401(k)
- All 50 states plus DC
- Export results to PDF, Excel (.xlsx) or CSV (in-browser)
- Send to phone as a plain-text note (share, copy, .txt or QR)

How to use:
1. Choose whether you are entering an hourly rate or a yearly salary.
2. Set hours per week, weeks worked, any overtime, and how often you are paid.
3. Pick your state and filing status to see gross and take-home pay for every period.

FAQ:

Q: How do hourly, overtime, and salary convert for 2026?
A: Straight time is hourly rate times hours per week times weeks worked. A $25 rate at 40 hours and 52 weeks is $52,000 a year, $1,000 a week, and $4,333.33 a month before tax. Overtime hours in this tool are paid at 1.5 times the hourly rate and are added before tax. Five overtime hours a week are 5 times $37.50 times 52 = $9,750, so gross becomes $61,750. A salary entered as a yearly amount is divided by the pay-period count you pick. The tool does not assume a bonus, shift differential, or a different overtime base. If your state or contract uses a weighted average for blended rates, calculate that hourly rate first and type it in.

Q: What does a $25-an-hour single paycheck look like in Texas?
A: Gross is $52,000. Federal taxable income after the 2026 standard deduction of $16,100 is $35,900. Tax is $1,240 plus 12 percent of $23,500, which is $2,820, for $4,060 of federal income tax. Social Security is $3,224 and Medicare is $754. Take-home pay for the year is $43,962 before health insurance or other deductions, or about $1,690.85 on each of 26 biweekly checks. The same gross paid semimonthly is 24 checks of about $1,831.75. Weekly is 52 checks of about $845.42. The annual tax does not change with frequency; only the size of each check does.

Q: Why is biweekly different from twice a month?
A: Biweekly means every two weeks, 26 pays in a normal year and 27 pays in some calendar years when a payday falls on January 1 or a leap pattern adds a check. Semimonthly means the 15th and the last day, always 24 pays. People who budget monthly often multiply a biweekly check by two and then feel short in the two months that have three checks. Multiply the biweekly net by 26 and divide by 12 to see a true monthly average. This calculator uses 26, 52, 24, or 12 exactly, and it does not move holidays to the previous business day.

Q: Which taxes come out, and which do not?
A: The engine uses the same 2026 federal brackets, standard deduction, state tables, Social Security wage base of $184,500, and Medicare rules as the income tax calculator. Pre-tax 401(k) contributions reduce income tax but not Social Security or Medicare, up to the $24,500 elective deferral cap modeled here. Health insurance, HSA contributions, garnishments, union dues, local taxes, and state paid-leave or disability premiums are not deducted. A W-2 employee should not also subtract self-employment tax. If you are both an owner and an employee, run wages here and estimate profit separately.

Q: How do I check the result against a pay stub?
A: Divide the year-to-date Social Security on a stub by 0.062. That implied wage base should be close to year-to-date gross if you are under $184,500 and have no pre-tax cafeteria plan that is exempt from FICA. Compare federal withholding with this estimate only after you account for the W-4: extra withholding, dependents, and a spouse's job move the stub away from a simple standard-deduction model. Use the calculator to plan a raise or a move between states, then confirm the first live stub. Export the schedule to Excel if you want the gross-to-net lines next to your budget.

Q: Does any of this leave my browser?
A: No. Hours, rate, state, and filing status are calculated locally. There is no sign-up and no payroll account. PDF, Excel, and CSV exports and the Send to phone note are created on your device. Do not send a note that includes a coworker's pay to a shared chat unless you mean to. The figures are planning estimates, not a paystub, a W-2, or tax advice.

Reference:

Gross-to-net reference Hourly gross is rate times hours per week times weeks per year. Overtime hours in this tool are paid at 1.5 times the straight rate and added before tax. A yearly salary is divided by 52 weekly, 26 biweekly, 24 semimonthly, or 12 monthly pays. Income tax uses the same 2026 federal and state tables as the income tax calculator . Payroll tax still applies to 401(k) deferrals. Health premiums, HSAs, local tax, and state disability insurance are not removed. Worked example: $25 an hour, 40 hours, 52 weeks, single, Texas Gross is $52,000. Federal tax after the $16,100 standard deduction is $4,060. Social Security is $3,224. Medicare is $754. Annual take-home is $43,962. Each biweekly check is about $1,690.85. Each semimonthly check is about $1,831.75. Five overtime hours a week add 5 times $37.50 times 52, or $9,750, before you rerun the tax. Pay-frequency traps Two biweekly checks are not a month. Multiply by 26 and divide by 12 for a monthly budget figure, about $3,663.51 in the example above. A year with 27 biweekly pay dates is a calendar accident this model does not invent; it always uses the count you select. Semimonthly is the 15th and the last day in real payroll and is simply one twenty-fourth of annual net here. Checking a stub Social Security year-to-date divided by 0.062 should be close to FICA wages if you are under the $184,500 wage base and have no pre-tax plan that is exempt from FICA. Federal withholding on a stub moves with the W-4. Use this page to compare states or a raise, then confirm the first live check. Pair the monthly net with the budget calculator .

### Loan Calculator

URL: https://greaterworldmedia.tech/loan-calculator/
Price: Free. Sign-up: not required. Processing: in your browser; files are not uploaded.

Calculate monthly payments, total interest and a full amortization schedule for business, equipment, SBA and mortgage loans. Extra payments supported. Free, no sign-up.

Features:
- Business, equipment, SBA 7(a) and mortgage presets
- Monthly payment and total interest
- Down payment
- Extra monthly payments and interest saved
- Yearly summary and full monthly amortization schedule
- Payoff date
- Export results to PDF, Excel (.xlsx) or CSV (in-browser)
- Send to phone as a plain-text note (share, copy, .txt or QR)

How to use:
1. Pick a loan type to load typical example values, then enter your own amount, rate and term.
2. Add a down payment or an extra monthly payment if you plan to make one.
3. Read the monthly payment, total interest and payoff date, and open the full schedule.

FAQ:

Q: Show the payment on a $50,000 business loan at 9 percent for 5 years.
A: The fixed monthly payment is P times r divided by 1 minus (1 plus r) to the minus n, where r is the annual rate divided by 12 and n is the number of months. Here r is 0.09 divided by 12 = 0.0075 and n is 60. The payment is $1,037.92. Over 60 months you pay about $62,275, of which about $12,275 is interest. The first month's interest is $50,000 times 0.0075 = $375.00, so about $662.92 of that first payment is principal. Interest falls each month as the balance falls. This is nominal monthly compounding of a fixed APR. It is not an interest-only period, a balloon, or a daily-accrual loan.

Q: What does an extra $100 a month change?
A: Adding $100 to the contractual payment on that same loan pays the loan off in 54 months instead of 60. Total interest falls to about $10,887.63, which is about $1,387.44 less than the original interest. The calculator applies the extra amount to principal after interest each month and stops when the balance is gone. It does not model a prepayment penalty. If your lender applies extra payments only once a year, the savings will be a little smaller than a monthly extra. Type the extra amount you will actually send, not an amount you hope to send.

Q: How do the presets differ from a quote?
A: Business, equipment, SBA 7(a), and mortgage presets only fill example price, down payment, rate, and term so you can see the shape of a schedule. They are not offers. A sample mortgage of a $400,000 price with $80,000 down is a $320,000 loan. At 6.5 percent for 30 years the principal-and-interest payment is about $2,022.62 and total interest is about $408,142. That payment excludes property tax, insurance, and mortgage insurance. An equipment preset with a down payment borrows price minus down payment. Replace the rate with the APR on your term sheet before you decide.

Q: What should I book, and what is missing?
A: Each payment splits into interest expense and a reduction of the loan liability. The yearly summary is a practical way to match a 12-month book close. The monthly schedule is the subledger. The tool does not add origination fees, points, or a separate amortization of closing costs, so the APR you were quoted may already differ from the note rate. Type the note rate if you want cash interest, or the APR if you want a single figure that folds some fees into the rate, and label which one you used in the export. Payments are assumed to start the month you pick and to stay fixed.

Q: Where does this differ from the small loan box on the business calculators page?
A: The business calculators page gives a payment, total paid, and total interest for a quick price. This page adds a down payment, extra principal, a payoff month, a yearly rollup, and every month of the schedule, and it exports that schedule. Use the quick box while you are guessing a term. Use this page when you are ready to show a lender, a partner, or your bookkeeper the month-by-month split. Both use the same standard formula.

Q: Are the loan details uploaded?
A: No. Amount, rate, term, and extra payment stay in the browser. PDF, Excel, and CSV files and the phone note are generated locally and include a line that fees, taxes, and insurance are excluded and that the result is not financial advice. There is no application and no credit check.

Reference:

Amortization formula The fixed payment is P times r divided by 1 minus (1 plus r) to the power of minus n. P is the amount borrowed, r is the annual rate divided by 12, and n is the number of months. Interest for a month is the opening balance times r. Principal is the payment minus that interest. An extra payment reduces principal after interest. The schedule stops when the balance is gone. Fees, taxes, insurance, and prepayment penalties are not added. Worked example: $50,000 at 9 percent for 5 years r is 0.0075 and n is 60. The payment is $1,037.92. Total interest is about $12,275. The first month's interest is $375.00, so about $662.92 is principal. An extra $100 a month finishes in 54 payments and saves about $1,387 of interest. A mortgage-shaped example, $320,000 at 6.5 percent for 30 years, is about $2,022.62 a month of principal and interest and about $408,142 of interest over the full term, before tax and insurance. How to read the schedule in the books Split each cash payment into interest expense and a reduction of the loan liability. The yearly summary matches a 12-month close. The monthly table is the subledger. Presets are example fillers, not credit offers. Type the note rate if you want cash interest, and label the export if you typed an APR that already folds in fees. For a one-line payment without a schedule, the loan box on the business calculators page uses the same formula.

### Profit Margin Calculator

URL: https://greaterworldmedia.tech/profit-margin/
Price: Free. Sign-up: not required. Processing: in your browser; files are not uploaded.

Calculate profit margin and markup, the selling price for a target margin, and break-even units and revenue. Free, instant, no sign-up.

Features:
- Margin and markup from cost and price
- Selling price from target margin or markup
- Price ladder for common margins
- Break-even units and revenue
- Units needed for a profit goal
- Contribution margin
- Export results to PDF, Excel (.xlsx) or CSV (in-browser)
- Send to phone as a plain-text note (share, copy, .txt or QR)

How to use:
1. Enter a cost and a selling price to see profit, margin and markup.
2. Enter a cost and a target margin (or markup) to get the selling price you need.
3. Enter fixed costs, price and variable cost per unit to find your break-even point.

FAQ:

Q: What is the difference between margin and markup on a $40 cost and a $65 price?
A: Profit is $25. Margin is profit divided by the selling price: 25 divided by 65 = 38.46 percent. Markup is profit divided by cost: 25 divided by 40 = 62.5 percent. A 50 percent markup on a $40 cost is a $60 price and only a 33.33 percent margin, because 20 divided by 60 is one third. Quoting markup when a buyer asked for margin is a common way to underprice. This page shows both from the same two numbers so you can answer either question without converting in your head.

Q: How do I set a price from a target margin, and what is a simple ROI check?
A: Price equals cost divided by 1 minus the target margin. A 40 percent margin on a $40 cost is 40 divided by 0.60 = $66.67. The same cost at a 40 percent markup is 40 times 1.40 = $56.00, which is only a 28.6 percent margin. A simple return on the inventory dollar, sometimes called markup ROI, is profit divided by cost, which is the markup itself: $26.67 profit on $66.67 is a 66.7 percent return on the $40 cost, not a 40 percent return. If you also spend $10 of shipping and fees that are not in cost, put them in cost before you divide or the margin will not survive the order.

Q: How many units cover $5,000 of fixed costs?
A: Break-even units equal fixed costs divided by price minus variable cost per unit, rounded up to a whole unit. At a $25 price and a $10 variable cost, contribution is $15. $5,000 divided by 15 is 333.33, so you need 334 units. Revenue at that point is 334 times $25 = $8,350. Contribution margin ratio is 15 divided by 25 = 60 percent. To clear an extra $3,000 profit goal, divide 8,000 by 15 and round up to 534 units. If price is not above variable cost, there is no break-even: every sale loses money.

Q: How should a product business use margin in its books?
A: Gross margin in the accounts is net sales minus cost of goods sold, divided by net sales. Cost of goods includes the unit you typed plus inbound freight and packaging if you cannot sell without them. Payment processing, marketplace fees, and discounts are often outside the unit cost people type here. A 38 percent calculator margin can become a 20 percent accounting margin after a 15 percent discount and a 3 percent card fee. Run the price on the discounted net and put the fee in variable cost. Review the ladder of common margins when a supplier raises cost so you can see the new price before you reprint labels.

Q: When should I use the combined business calculators instead?
A: Use the four-in-one business calculators page for a fast margin, a single sales-tax line, a loan payment, or a monthly break-even while you are in a meeting. Use this page when you need the price for a target markup, the price ladder, a profit goal above break-even, and an export you can attach to a pricing memo. The formulas match. The dedicated page keeps the three questions side by side so changing cost updates the ladder.

Q: Do my costs get stored?
A: No. Cost, price, and fixed costs are calculated on the device. You can download PDF, Excel, or CSV or send a text note to your phone. There is no account. The result is a pricing aid, not a financial statement or tax advice.

Reference:

Margin, markup, price, and break-even Margin is profit divided by price. Markup is profit divided by cost. Price for a target margin is cost divided by 1 minus the margin. Price for a target markup is cost times 1 plus the markup. Break-even units are fixed costs divided by price minus variable cost, rounded up. A simple return on the unit cost is profit divided by cost, which is the markup, not the margin. Worked example Cost $40 and price $65: profit $25, margin 38.46 percent, markup 62.5 percent. A 40 percent margin on that cost needs 40 divided by 0.60, or $66.67. A 40 percent markup needs only $56.00 and yields a 28.6 percent margin. Fixed costs of $5,000, price $25, variable cost $10: contribution is $15, so break-even is 334 units and $8,350 of revenue. A further $3,000 profit goal needs 534 units. Where the margin goes Discounts and card fees are often missing from the unit cost people type. A 15 percent discount and a 3 percent fee can turn a 38 percent calculator margin into something near 20 percent in the accounts. Put inbound freight in cost if you cannot sell without it. Gross margin in the ledger is net sales minus cost of goods sold, divided by net sales. The price ladder shows common target margins on the cost you typed. The business calculators page is the same margin math without the ladder. The freelance rate calculator is the service-business version, where the cost is your year rather than a unit.

### Receipt & Quote Maker

How to use:
1. Choose Receipt, Estimate or Quote and enter your business and customer details.
2. Add line items, then set any discount, tax rate and (for quotes) a deposit.
3. Print or save the document as a PDF, or export the data to Excel or CSV.

FAQ:

Q: What is the difference between a receipt, an estimate, and a quote?
A: A receipt records money you already took, including the payment method. An estimate is an approximate price that can move when the scope becomes clearer. A quote is a fixed offer, usually with a valid-until date. After the client accepts, you invoice the work; this page does not convert the file automatically, so create the invoice from the same lines. Putting Estimate on a fixed price, or Quote on a guess, causes arguments. The heading on the PDF follows the type you pick.

Q: How are discount, tax, and deposit calculated?
A: The discount reduces the subtotal first. Tax is calculated on the discounted amount, which matches how most US sales-tax rules treat a cash discount. A $500 subtotal with a 10 percent discount is $450, and 8 percent tax is $36, for $486. A deposit on a quote is an amount due to start, not a second tax. The balance is the total minus the deposit. Do not tax the deposit again when you invoice the balance. If a line is exempt, handle the tax rate so you do not tax that whole document, or split the exempt work onto its own document.

Q: What dates and numbers should I print?
A: Quotes need a valid-until date so the price can expire when your supplier's price expires. Estimates should say they are approximate if the job can change. Receipts need the date paid and the method, such as card or bank transfer, so the client's books and yours match. Keep a separate sequence from invoices if you must, but do not reuse a number. The PDF is the copy you send; the Excel or CSV export is the copy you file.

Q: How do I move from a quote to money in the bank?
A: Send the quote PDF. When the client accepts, take the deposit you stated, then invoice the remainder with the invoice generator using the same line descriptions. On the day you are paid in full, a receipt closes the loop. None of these documents file sales tax for you. The sales tax calculator is where you check the rate and the exempt lines before you type the percent. A quote is not revenue. Book a deposit as a liability until you do the work if you keep accrual records.

Q: Can I add a logo?
A: This version is text on purpose so it prints cleanly and does not depend on a hosted image. Make a logo in the logo maker and use it on your site and cards. If you later paste a logo into another template, host the image yourself or the client's mail app will show a broken picture. There is no watermark on these PDFs.

Q: Are customer details uploaded?
A: No. Names, prices, and notes stay in the browser until you download or print. PDF, Excel, and CSV and the phone note are created locally. There is no account. Do not use Send to phone on a shared device if the note contains a customer's address.

Reference:

Receipt, estimate, and quote A receipt proves payment and should name the method. An estimate is allowed to move when the job becomes clearer. A quote is a fixed offer with a valid-until date. Tax is computed after the discount, which is the order most US sales-tax rules expect. A deposit is an amount due to start, not a second taxable sale. The balance is the total minus the deposit. Worked example A $500 subtotal with a 10 percent discount is $450. Tax at 8 percent is $36. The total is $486. A $150 deposit leaves a $336 balance to invoice later. Do not tax the deposit again on the final invoice. If the valid-until date passes and your supplier price moved, send a new quote rather than honoring a dead number by accident. From quote to books A quote is not revenue. A deposit you have not earned is a liability if you keep accrual records. When the client accepts, create the invoice on the invoice generator with the same lines. Check the rate on the sales tax calculator before you type the percent, especially if one line is exempt. ### Freelance Rate Calculator

URL: https://greaterworldmedia.tech/freelance-rate/
Price: Free. Sign-up: not required. Processing: in your browser; files are not uploaded.

Calculate your freelance hourly, day and project rate from target income, expenses, taxes, time off and billable hours. Free, private, no sign-up.

Features:
- Hourly, day, weekly and monthly rates
- Project price from estimated hours
- Target take-home income
- Business expenses and tax estimate
- Billable percentage and time off
- Profit buffer
- Export results to PDF, Excel (.xlsx) or CSV (in-browser)
- Send to phone as a plain-text note (share, copy, .txt or QR)

How to use:
1. Enter the yearly income you want to take home and your yearly business expenses.
2. Set your estimated tax rate, working weeks, hours per week and the share of hours you can bill.
3. Read your minimum hourly, day and project rates, then round up when you quote.

FAQ:

Q: Walk through the default rate: $60,000 take-home, 25 percent tax, $10,000 costs.
A: First gross the take-home up for tax: $60,000 divided by 1 minus 0.25 = $80,000 you must bill before tax. Add $10,000 of business expenses to get $90,000. A 10 percent profit buffer multiplies that by 1.10, so you need $99,000 of revenue. Working 48 weeks at 40 hours is 1,920 hours. At a 70 percent billable share you can invoice 1,344 hours. $99,000 divided by 1,344 is $73.66 an hour. An 8-hour day is about $589. A 20-hour project is about $1,473 before you round. Round up to a number you will actually quote, such as $75 or $80, because scope grows and some hours will not be billed.

Q: What does the 25 percent tax box represent, and what does it miss?
A: It is a planning reserve, not a filed return. US self-employed people generally pay self-employment tax of 15.3 percent on 92.35 percent of net profit, plus federal income tax and often state income tax. On $80,000 of net profit, self-employment tax alone is about $11,304 before the deduction for half of it. A 25 to 35 percent combined reserve is a common planning range, but a high-earning filer in a high-tax state can need more, and a low-profit year can need less. The box does not compute the qualified business income deduction, the home-office deduction, or quarterly vouchers. Revisit it after you see last year's effective rate, and use the 2026 wage calculator only for W-2 pay, not for this profit.

Q: Why is 100 percent of my week not billable?
A: Proposals, email, invoicing, bookkeeping, and learning are real work and they are usually not on the invoice. 60 to 75 percent billable is a realistic band for an independent who also sells the work. 70 percent of a 40-hour week is 28 billable hours. If you type 100 percent, the hourly rate looks comfortingly low and you will miss the income target as soon as a week includes a sales call. Time off is handled by working weeks: 48 weeks leaves about four weeks for holidays, illness, and a short break. If you take eight weeks off, drop working weeks to 44 and let the rate rise.

Q: How do I turn the hourly rate into a project quote?
A: Estimate the hours honestly, including revisions and project management, then multiply by the hourly rate. A job you think is 20 hours at $73.66 is about $1,473, and a 15 percent revision buffer makes it about $1,694. Fixed bids should use the buffered number, not the best case. Day rates assume a full day; if the client only books two hours, the day rate divided by eight underprices the context-switching. The tool shows hourly, day, weekly, and project figures from the same revenue target so you do not invent a second rate.

Q: What expenses belong in the yearly cost box?
A: Software, insurance, equipment you will replace this year, contractor help, accounting, and a modest marketing budget. Do not put your personal rent in the box unless a real portion is a deductible office you would not pay otherwise; mixing household costs into the rate is fine for personal planning but label it so you do not treat it as a business deduction. Owner draws are not an expense. The income box is what you want to keep after tax, so do not also add your draw as a cost or you will double count it.

Q: Is this rate stored anywhere?
A: No. Income, costs, tax percent, and hours stay in the browser. Export PDF, Excel, or CSV, or send a note to your phone, from the page itself. There is no profile and no marketplace listing. The rate is a planning figure, not a contract and not tax advice.

Reference:

The rate formula Gross the income you want to keep by dividing by 1 minus your tax reserve. Add yearly business expenses. Multiply by 1 plus the profit buffer. Divide by billable hours, which are working weeks times hours per week times the billable share. Day rate is hourly times a full day. A project price is hourly times the hours you will actually spend, including revisions. Worked example using the defaults $60,000 take-home at a 25 percent reserve is $80,000 before tax. Plus $10,000 of costs is $90,000. A 10 percent buffer makes $99,000 of revenue to bill. 48 weeks times 40 hours times 70 percent is 1,344 billable hours. The floor is $73.66 an hour, about $589 a day, and about $1,473 for a 20-hour project before you round up. Quoting $75 or $80 leaves room for scope you did not write down. Tax reserve versus a W-2 calculator The percent is a planning reserve. On $80,000 of self-employment profit, self-employment tax alone is about 15.3 percent of 92.35 percent, or about $11,304, before income tax and before the deduction for half of that tax. The wage calculator does not compute that. Owner draws are not an expense. Typing 100 percent billable underprices the week you spend on proposals. Use the invoice generator to bill the rate you settled, and the budget calculator to park the tax reserve as a need.

### Sales Tax Calculator

URL: https://greaterworldmedia.tech/sales-tax/
Price: Free. Sign-up: not required. Processing: in your browser; files are not uploaded.

Calculate sales tax for any US state with 2026 state and average local rates. Reverse sales tax from a total, multiple items, non-taxable lines. Free, instant, no sign-up.

Features:
- 2026 state and average local rates for all 50 states and DC
- Reverse sales tax: find the pre-tax price from a total
- Multiple items with quantities
- Non-taxable lines (for example gift cards or exempt goods)
- Custom exact rate for your city or county
- Compare tax on the same purchase across every state
- Export results to PDF, Excel (.xlsx) or CSV (in-browser)
- Send to phone as a plain-text note (share, copy, .txt or QR)

How to use:
1. Pick your state and the rate to use. For an exact rate, choose "My exact rate" and enter the combined rate from your receipt or your state revenue department.
2. Choose whether the prices you enter are before tax or already include tax.
3. List the items with quantity and price, untick "Taxable" for any exempt item, and read the tax and total.

FAQ:

Q: How do I add sales tax, with a real receipt example?
A: Tax equals the taxable amount times the rate as a decimal. At a combined 8.25 percent, tax on $100.00 is $8.25 and the customer pays $108.25. On three taxable items of $24.00, $10.50, and $6.00 the taxable base is $40.50 and the tax is $3.34125, which you should round to the cent the way your state requires, usually $3.34, for a total of $43.84. This tool rounds money to the cent on line amounts and on the tax result. If one line is a gift card or a labor charge your state exempts, untick Taxable so it stays in the total but out of the tax base.

Q: How do I remove tax that is already in the price?
A: Divide the tax-inclusive total by 1 plus the rate. A shelf price of $108.25 at 8.25 percent is $108.25 divided by 1.0825 = $100.00 before tax, so the embedded tax is $8.25. A $249.99 total at the same rate is $249.99 divided by 1.0825 = $230.94 before tax and $19.05 of tax, after cent rounding. Choose Tax included in the tool when the number on the tag already contains tax. Do not also multiply that tag price by the rate or you will tax the tax.

Q: Why does my city's rate differ from the state average?
A: The state rate in the table is the statewide rate. The local figure is a population-weighted average of city, county, and special-district rates published by the Tax Foundation as of July 1, 2026, not the rate at one address. Texas, for example, is 6.25 percent state plus about 1.95 percent average local, or 8.20 percent combined, but a specific city can be higher or lower. Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon have no statewide sales tax; Alaska's local average is about 1.82 percent. Choose My exact rate and type the combined rate from your state's rate lookup or from a recent receipt when you are charging a customer.

Q: What should a shop record for sales tax payable?
A: Sales tax you collect is not revenue. Book the pre-tax price as sales and the tax as a liability until you remit it. If you give a discount, this tool follows the usual US order: discount reduces the subtotal, then tax is computed on the discounted taxable amount. Exempt sales still belong in gross receipts if your state return asks for them, but they are not in the tax you owe. Use the compare-by-state table only to see how the same basket changes across states. It is not a nexus study. Shipping, freight, and digitally delivered goods are taxable in some states and not others, so confirm the category before you file.

Q: How do state and average local rates get updated?
A: Rates in the menu come from the Tax Foundation 2026 sales tax rates midyear update, rates as of July 1, 2026, with state rates cross-checked against the Foundation's state sales tax table. We do not scrape a live rate API at the moment you calculate, which is why an exact city rate belongs in My exact rate. When a state changes its rate, the published table and this page are updated together. The page states the as-of date next to the source link. Food, clothing, and services can be taxed at a different rate or exempt even when the general rate is correct.

Q: Is the basket I type sent to a server?
A: No. Items, quantities, prices, and the rate are processed in the page. You can export the result as PDF, Excel, or CSV, or send a plain-text note to your phone, all created in the browser. There is no account. The rate source link goes to the Tax Foundation; following it leaves this site and is covered by their policy, not by a data upload of your basket.

Reference:

Sales-tax arithmetic for 2026 Added tax is the taxable base times the rate. Tax included in the price comes back out by dividing by 1 plus the rate. The state rate in the menu is exact. The local add-on is the Tax Foundation population-weighted average as of July 1, 2026, not the rate at one street address. Type My exact rate when you are charging a customer. The published source is the Tax Foundation 2026 midyear sales-tax update . Worked examples at 8.25 percent On $100.00, tax is $8.25 and the customer pays $108.25. Working backwards, $108.25 divided by 1.0825 returns $100.00. On $249.99 tax-inclusive, the pre-tax price is $249.99 divided by 1.0825, or $230.94, and the tax is $19.05 after cent rounding. Three lines of $24.00, $10.50, and $6.00 are a $40.50 base and $3.34 of tax if you round the tax to the cent. An unticked Taxable line stays in the amount due and out of the base. States with no statewide tax Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon have a zero statewide rate in this table. Alaska still has local tax, averaging about 1.82 percent. A zero state rate is not a promise that your city is zero. Food, clothing, freight, and services are often exempt or taxed at another rate even when the general rate is right. Bookkeeping Record the pre-tax amount as sales and the tax as a liability until you remit it. Discount the subtotal before you compute tax, which is what the receipt and quote maker does. The compare-all-states table shows the same basket at each combined average. It is not a nexus opinion. Use the invoice generator when you need the tax as a single rate on a document.

## Audio & Video

### Audio Converter & Ringtone Trimmer

URL: https://greaterworldmedia.tech/audio/
Price: Free. Sign-up: not required. Processing: in your browser; files are not uploaded.

Trim audio, add fade in/out and export MP3 or WAV ringtones free. No sign-up and no upload: your files never leave your device.

Features:
- Trim audio with start/end sliders
- Fade in and fade out
- Export MP3 or WAV
- Ringtone length presets
- No upload: runs in the browser

How to use:
1. Open an audio file from your device.
2. Drag the start and end sliders, and add a fade in or out.
3. Preview, then export as MP3 or WAV.

FAQ:

Q: MP3 or WAV, and what does this trimmer actually export?
A: WAV is the uncompressed PCM of the selection, stereo or mono as in the file, at the file's own sample rate, 16-bit. It is the right export when you will edit again. MP3 is encoded in the browser at a fixed 128 kbps with the bundled LAME encoder, which is a small file and plenty for a ringtone or a voice memo. This page does not offer 192 or 320 kbps. If you need a higher-bitrate MP3, export WAV and encode elsewhere, or use the video-to-MP3 tool when the source is a video and you want 192 or 320. A one-minute stereo WAV at 44.1 kHz is about 10 MB. The same minute as 128 kbps MP3 is about 1 MB.

Q: How long should a ringtone or alert be, and how do fades work?
A: Most phones are happy with 20 to 30 seconds. iPhone ringtone files are limited to about 30 seconds, so set the end point at or before 30 if that is the destination. A 1 to 2 second fade-out keeps the clip from clicking at the end. Fade-in can be shorter, often under a second, unless you are softening a loud attack. The fade is a gain ramp on the samples you selected, not a separate effect track. Preview before you export. The selection cannot be shorter than a tenth of a second.

Q: Which files open, and what if decode fails?
A: The browser's audio decoder has to understand the file. MP3, WAV, M4A, AAC, OGG, and FLAC open in current browsers when the codec is supported. A file over about 200 MB is rejected so the tab does not run out of memory. If decode fails, the audio may be corrupt or use a codec the browser cannot play. Convert that file to WAV or MP3 on a machine that can play it, then trim here. The page does not download audio from a URL, a streaming site, or YouTube. It only reads a file you already have.

Q: What are the rights and the privacy limits?
A: Trim audio you own or have a license to use. A purchased song is often licensed for personal listening, not for a remix you publish. This tool will not stop you, and it also will not fetch the song for you. Processing is local. The waveform is drawn from the samples on your device. There is no account and no upload. Export before you close the tab. Memory errors on long files are solved by a shorter selection or by exporting WAV in smaller pieces, not by sending the file to us.

Q: How do I make a clean clip for a podcast or a hold message?
A: Set the start just before the first word and the end just after the last, then add a short fade so you do not cut a breath in half. Voice is intelligible at 128 kbps mono or stereo. Leave the original untrimmed file in your archive. Do not normalize or remove noise here; this page trims and fades only. If the level is too low, fix it in an editor before you export the master. The sample rate of the export matches the source, so a 48 kHz interview stays 48 kHz.

Q: Why does the MP3 sound duller than the WAV?
A: 128 kbps throws away some high-frequency detail. On a phone speaker you will rarely hear it. On studio monitors, a music clip will sound tighter in the WAV. Choose WAV when the next step is editing or a master, and MP3 when the file has to be small. Re-encoding an MP3 to MP3 again makes the loss worse. Trim from WAV or from the original when you can.

Reference:

Trim, fade, WAV, and 128 kbps MP3 The selection is a start time and an end time on the file you open. Fades are gain ramps on those samples. WAV export is 16-bit PCM at the source sample rate, mono or stereo as decoded. MP3 export is a fixed 128 kbps file from the in-browser LAME encoder. There is no 192 or 320 option on this page. The page does not fetch audio from a URL. Ringtone and voice targets A phone ringtone wants about 20 to 30 seconds. iPhone ringtones are limited to about 30 seconds, so set the end at or before 30. A 1 to 2 second fade-out stops a click. Voice is fine at 128 kbps. A minute of stereo WAV at 44.1 kHz is about 10 MB. The same minute at 128 kbps is about 1 MB. Preview the selection. The shortest cut is a tenth of a second. Files over about 200 MB are rejected so the tab does not die, and decode fails when the browser does not know the codec. Rights and the next edit Trim files you own or may use. Re-encoding MP3 to MP3 makes music duller. Trim from WAV when you can, and keep the WAV if you will edit again. For a video source and a higher MP3 bitrate, use video to MP3 , which offers 128, 192, and 320. This page only trims and fades. It does not denoise or normalize.

2. Read the live counts for words, characters, sentences and paragraphs.
3. Check reading time and top keywords.

FAQ:

Q: How are words, characters, and time counted?
A: Words are split on whitespace, so a hyphenated word is one word and a number is a word. Characters are shown with spaces and without them. Sentences are split on end punctuation. Paragraphs are blocks separated by blank lines. Reading time uses about 238 words per minute. Speaking time uses about 150 words per minute. A 600-word product description is about 2.5 minutes to read and about 4 minutes to read aloud. Those rates are averages for adult English, not a promise about your reader. The top-keyword list skips very common function words so you can see what you actually repeat.

Q: What lengths matter for real business writing?
A: A search snippet is often cut near 150 to 160 characters, so write the meta description in this box and watch the character count with spaces. Many ad headlines are tighter than 30 characters. A short email people will finish is often under 200 words. A blog post that teaches something real is commonly 800 to 1,500 words, which is a reading time of roughly 4 to 7 minutes at 238 words per minute. The counter does not judge quality. It stops you from discovering the limit after you have pasted into an ad platform.

Q: What does keyword repetition tell you, and what does it not?
A: If one product name is 8 percent of the words, the paragraph may be stuffing rather than explaining. If the name never appears, the page may be vague. The list is a frequency count, not a ranking score and not a guarantee that a search engine will treat the phrase as a topic. Proper names and SKUs count. The same word with different capitalization is grouped in the usual way the counter normalizes. Use it to edit, then read the paragraph aloud.

Q: How should I use it with the resume and policy tools?
A: Resume bullets should usually be one or two lines, roughly 15 to 30 words. Paste a bullet here if you cannot tell whether it is bloated. Policy drafts from the policy generator run long because they have to cover topics; the counter tells you the length so you can see whether a section became a wall of text. Neither tool sends the text to the other. Copy and paste is the handoff, and it stays on the device.

Q: Are there limits on length?
A: Very large pastes are counted locally and can take a moment. The page is built to handle a long document without uploading it. If the tab becomes slow, split the text. There is no account and no stored document. Export PDF, Excel, or CSV if you want the counts and the keyword list in a file, or send a note to your phone. The export is the counts, not a backup of a novel, unless the text is included in that export's inputs.

Q: Does it count HTML, code, or languages other than English?
A: Tags and code are counted as they appear. A page of HTML will show a high word count that includes tags, which is not the reading length of the visible article. Paste the visible text if that is what you care about. Languages without spaces between words will not match an English word count; the character count is still meaningful. Emoji and accents count as characters. The reading-time constant is still the English average.

Reference:

Counts that match the way editors talk Words split on whitespace. Characters are reported with spaces and without. Reading time uses about 238 words per minute. Speaking time uses about 150. A 600-word description is about two and a half minutes to read and about four minutes to speak. The keyword list skips common function words. HTML pasted from a template counts the tags, so paste the visible text if you want a reading length. Lengths businesses actually hit Meta descriptions are often cut near 150 to 160 characters. Many ad headlines sit under 30 characters. A short email that gets finished is often under 200 words. A teaching article commonly runs 800 to 1,500 words, or about four to seven minutes at 238 words per minute. Resume bullets are healthier at one or two lines, roughly 15 to 30 words. Paste a bullet from the resume tool if you cannot tell whether it has swollen. None of these are scores. They are limits you would rather see here than in a rejected upload. What the keyword list will not do Frequency is not a ranking. A product name at 8 percent of the words may be stuffing. A name that never appears may be a vague page. Languages that do not put spaces between words will not match an English word count. The character count still means something. Exports save the counts locally. The text itself never needs an account, and it is not uploaded.

### Resume Bullet Improver

URL: https://greaterworldmedia.tech/resume/
Price: Free. Sign-up: not required. Processing: in your browser; files are not uploaded.

Turn plain job duties into clear, quantified resume bullet points free. No sign-up; your text stays private in your browser.

Features:
- Action-verb bullet rewrites
- Add numbers and results
- Several verb styles
- Copy bullets
- Export results to PDF or Excel (.xlsx) (in-browser)
- Send to phone as a plain-text note (share, copy, .txt or QR)

How to use:
1. Paste a plain job duty, such as “handled customer emails”.
2. Choose a verb style and add a number and a result if you have them.
3. Copy the bullet that fits best and adjust the details.

FAQ:

Q: What does a strong bullet contain?
A: A strong bullet starts with an action verb, names the work, and ends with a result a stranger can picture. Handled customer emails is a duty. Answered about 40 customer emails a day and cut the average reply time from a day to under four hours is a bullet. The number can be volume, money, time, or a percent. If you do not have a measured result, use an honest scope: a team of four, a territory of 30 accounts, a class of 25. Do not invent a percentage. Interviewers ask, and a fabricated metric is worse than a plain true sentence.

Q: How many bullets, and in what order?
A: Three to five bullets for a recent role is typical. Older roles can have fewer. Put the result that best matches the job you want first, not the task you did most often. A one-page resume for early career and a two-page resume for a long career are both normal. This tool rewrites one duty at a time so you can paste the best line back into your document. It does not design the page, and it does not invent employers.

Q: How do I use numbers I am not sure of?
A: Use ranges you can defend: about 200 tickets a week, roughly $40,000 in renewals, a queue that fell by around a third. If you cannot defend it, leave the number out. Look at old reports, a CRM export, or a calendar before you guess. The word counter will tell you if a bullet has grown past two lines. A bullet that needs a semicolon and three clauses is usually two bullets.

Q: What should stay out of the bullet?
A: Pronouns, soft skills with no evidence, and the company's marketing slogan. References available upon request is wasted space. Graphics and photos are a liability in many US hiring pipelines and can confuse applicant-tracking systems that read text. Keep the file as text. Do not put a password, a social security number, or a client's confidential metric in a bullet you will upload to a job site.

Q: How do the verb styles differ?
A: The styles change the opening verb so you can hear more than one tone. Pick the one that sounds like the work, then edit the rest of the sentence so the verb agrees with the facts. A louder verb does not make a weak result strong. If none of the lines are true, rewrite the duty more specifically and run it again. The tool is a prompt for clarity, not a biography.

Q: Is my work history uploaded?
A: No. The duty you paste is rewritten in the browser. There is no account and no profile. PDF and Excel exports are local. Clear the box when you are done on a shared computer. The text is only as private as the device and the file you download.

Reference:

Duties into bullets Lead with a verb, name the work, and stop on a result a stranger can picture. Volume, money, time, or a percent all count. If you cannot measure the result, state an honest scope: a team of four, 30 accounts, a class of 25. Three to five bullets for a recent role is enough. Put the line that matches the job you want first. This page rewrites one duty at a time. It does not lay out the page and it does not invent employers. Before and after Handled customer emails is a duty. Answered about 40 customer emails a day and cut the typical reply from a day to under four hours is a bullet, if both numbers are true. About 200 tickets a week is fair when you can show the queue. A 40 percent improvement you cannot explain is not. Look at a CRM export or a calendar before you guess. A bullet that needs three clauses is usually two bullets. The word counter will show when a line has passed about 30 words. What to leave out Pronouns, slogans, and references available upon request. Do not put a client's confidential metric, a password, or a government ID in a file you will upload to a job site. Keep the resume as text so an applicant-tracking system can read it. The verb styles only change the opening. Edit the rest until the sentence is something you will say out loud in an interview. The rewrite stays in the browser.

## Security

### Password Generator

URL: https://greaterworldmedia.tech/password/
Price: Free. Sign-up: not required. Processing: in your browser; files are not uploaded.

Generate strong random passwords free with a cryptographically secure generator. No sign-up; passwords are created on your device and never stored.

Features:
- Cryptographically secure randomness
- Custom length and character sets
- Strength estimate
- Nothing stored

How to use:
1. Choose a length (16 or more is recommended).
2. Pick which character types to include.
3. Copy one of the generated passwords.

FAQ:

Q: How random is a password from this page?
A: Each character is chosen with the browser's crypto.getRandomValues, which is a cryptographic generator, not Math.random. Selection is unbiased across the set you turned on. A 16-character password drawn from about 95 printable characters has on the order of 100 bits of entropy, because each character adds about 6.6 bits. Turn off symbols and you reduce the bits per character. Turn the length down to 8 and you cut the space in half in bit terms, which is a large cut, not a small one. The strength line is an entropy estimate of the settings, not a check against a list of leaked passwords.

Q: How long should it be, and should I reuse it?
A: Use at least 12 to 16 characters for ordinary accounts and longer for email, banking, and the password manager itself. A unique password per account matters more than a clever word. Reuse means one leak opens every site that shares the password. This page does not store the password, does not put it in an export, and does not offer Send to phone, because a notes file or a QR code of a password is a copy you will forget you made. Put it in a password manager. The manager is the memory.

Q: What should I do with the result?
A: Copy it once into the account you are creating and into the password manager. Do not email it to yourself. Do not paste it into a chat with a vendor. If a site rejects symbols, turn symbols off and add length until the strength line is still in the strong range, rather than shortening a complex password to 8 characters. A passphrase of several random words can be appropriate where you must type it often; this generator builds a random string, which is the better shape for a manager-filled login.

Q: What does the page refuse to do?
A: It will not generate a password if every character set is off, because there is nothing to draw from. It does not invent a memorable sentence. It does not check whether a particular site's rules require a number. If a site demands a number, leave digits on. The password is shown so you can copy it. Anyone who can see your screen can see it. Generate it when you are ready to store it, then clear the page if you are on a shared machine.

Q: How does this compare with a website's own generator?
A: A generator on a sign-up form may be fine, and it may also be a script you cannot read. This one is local and does not send the result to GWB. That does not make the password stronger than the math of its length and alphabet. A 6-character password generated perfectly is still short. Prefer this page or your manager's generator over a password built from a pet name and a year.

Q: Is anything stored?
A: No password is written to local storage, to an export file, or to a server. There is no account. Reloading the page gives a new set. If you needed the previous one and did not save it in your manager, it is gone, which is the intended failure mode.

Reference:

Entropy, length, and where the secret should live Characters come from crypto.getRandomValues, not from a guessable clock. A 16-character password from about 95 printable symbols carries on the order of 100 bits, about 6.6 bits per character. Cut the length to 8 and you cut that space in half in bit terms. Turn symbols off and each character is worth less, so add length until the strength line is still strong. The line estimates the settings. It does not search breach lists. A usable policy for a small team 16 characters or more, a unique password for every account, stored in a password manager. The email account and the manager's own master password should be longer. If a site rejects symbols, keep digits on and lengthen the password rather than dropping to 8 characters. This page will not export or send the password to a phone, because a notes file is a copy you will lose track of. Copy it into the manager and the account, then leave the page. Reloading throws the secret away on purpose. What the generator will not pretend It does not make a memorable sentence. It does not know a particular site's rules beyond the sets you enable. It does not upload the result, and there is no account to recover it from. A perfectly random 6-character password is still short. Prefer this page or the manager's generator over a pet's name and a year.
